snippet.title: The Most Brutal Parking Lot Assassination in Chicago Mob History
snippet.description:
He was not a street boss. He did not carry a gun, run a crew, or sit in the back of a social club barking orders. But Allen Dorfman may have been more valuable to the mob than most killers. He controlled access to money — Teamsters money, pension money, casino money — and for years, that made him one of the most dangerous men in the Chicago Outfit’s world.

Allen Dorfman was the man who helped turn union power into underworld wealth. Through the Teamsters Central States Pension Fund, millions of dollars flowed into Las Vegas casinos, mob-connected businesses, and hidden deals that made powerful people richer than the public ever knew. He was close to Jimmy Hoffa, connected to the Chicago Outfit, and trusted by men who did not trust easily.

But money men become dangerous when they know too much.

In December 1982, Dorfman was convicted in a federal corruption case involving Teamsters power, organized crime influence, and an alleged plan to bribe a United States senator. He was facing decades in prison. Prosecutors believed he had secrets. The Outfit believed he might talk. And before Allen Dorfman could face his own judgment day in court, someone made sure he never reached sentencing.

What you will learn in this documentary:
How Allen Dorfman became one of the most important money men in the Chicago Outfit’s orbit
Why his father Paul “Red” Dorfman helped connect him to Jimmy Hoffa and union power
How the Teamsters Central States Pension Fund became a gold mine for mob-connected loans
Why Las Vegas casinos depended on union pension money to expand
How Dorfman became tied to the casino skim era that inspired Casino
Why mob bosses valued financial operators as much as street enforcers
How Allen Dorfman moved between insurance, labor unions, Teamsters influence, and organized crime
Why federal investigators launched Operation Pendorf to penetrate his world
How hidden microphones inside his insurance office helped build the case against him
Why Dorfman’s conviction in 1982 terrified the men around him
How Joseph “Joey the Clown” Lombardo and Roy Williams became connected to the corruption case
Why Dorfman’s murder looked like a warning to anyone thinking about cooperating
How his death became one of the clearest examples of the mob silencing its own money man

Key figures:
Allen Dorfman, Paul “Red” Dorfman, Jimmy Hoffa, Roy Lee Williams, Joseph “Joey the Clown” Lombardo, Tony Accardo, Jackie Cerone, Joseph Aiuppa, Allen Glick, Frank “Lefty” Rosenthal, Tony Spilotro, Frank Balistrieri, Sidney Korshak, Howard Cannon, the Chicago Outfit, the Teamsters Central States Pension Fund

Timeline:
1923 birth of Allen Dorfman in Chicago, 1940s and 1950s Paul Dorfman rises through Teamsters insurance connections, 1950s Allen Dorfman becomes close to Jimmy Hoffa’s union world, 1960s Teamsters pension money flows into Las Vegas casino development, 1972 Dorfman is convicted in a pension-fund kickback case, 1975 Dorfman is tried and acquitted in a fraud case, 1979 FBI launches Operation Pendorf, May 1981 Dorfman and others are indicted in the bribery conspiracy case, December 1982 Dorfman is convicted with Roy Williams and Joseph Lombardo, January 20 1983 Dorfman is shot to death outside the Lincolnwood Hyatt, January 1983 his scheduled sentencing never happens.

Why this story matters today:
Allen Dorfman’s story matters because it shows that the Mafia was not built only on guns, fear, and street violence. It was built on banks, unions, insurance deals, pension funds, lawyers, casinos, and men who knew how to move money without leaving obvious fingerprints. Dorfman made the mob rich because he understood the hidden machinery behind power. But when prison threatened to turn that knowledge into testimony, the same world he helped finance turned on him. He made the mob rich — then they killed him before judgment day.

snippet.title: Why the Chicago Mafia Erased Their Own Underboss
snippet.description:
August thirty first, two thousand and six. Chicago Outfit Underboss Anthony Zizzo left his home for a routine meeting and was never seen again. His locked Jeep was left in a restaurant parking lot—no blood, no struggle, no clues. He was a ghost.

This wasn't a random crime. It was a highly orchestrated corporate assassination over a multi million dollar video poker empire. When the FBI locked up the top bosses during the infamous Family Secrets trial, a power vacuum triggered a vicious shadow war. Zizzo stood his ground against a ruthless rival faction. It was a fatal mistake.

What you will learn in this episode:

The exact mechanics of the mob's illegal video poker scheme and how it generated millions in untraceable cash.

How the "Family Secrets" indictments caused the Chicago Outfit to turn on its own leadership.

The psychological tactics used to lure a paranoid, high ranking Mafia boss out of hiding.

Why the FBI suspects Michael "The Large Guy" Sarno orchestrated the ultimate vanishing act.

The forensic reality of the abandoned Jeep and the decades long search for Zizzo's body.

Timeline & Key Figures:

Anthony "Little Tony" Zizzo: The 71 year old Underboss who controlled the western suburbs.

James Marcello: The Boss whose imprisonment sparked a deadly turf war.

Michael Sarno: The 300 pound Cicero enforcer who launched a hostile takeover.

This story matters today because it exposes the cold, corporate reality of modern organized crime. The flashy mobsters of the past are gone, replaced by calculating operators who understand that a missing person is much harder to prosecute than a murder victim.

Sources: FBI Chicago Field Office Records, United States vs. Sarno Court Transcripts, Chicago Tribune Investigative Archives.

snippet.title: La noche que POPEYE casi MATA a ESCOBAR
snippet.description:
Había una regla dentro del Cartel de Medellín que todos conocían pero nadie se atrevía a pronunciar en voz alta: cerca de Escobar no existían los errores. Sin embargo, hubo una noche que desafió esa ley no escrita de una manera que pocos creyeron posible. Una noche en que Popeye, el sicario más temido del cartel, estuvo a un solo reflejo de matar a Pablo Escobar por accidente.

En este vídeo te contamos todo lo que ocurrió durante aquellas horas de tensión extrema. Para entenderlo, hay que conocer el contexto: no estamos hablando del Escobar de las fiestas y el poder ilimitado, sino del Escobar acorralado, paranoico, durmiendo con un ojo abierto en casas de seguridad que cambiaba casi cada noche. Un hombre que ya no distinguía con claridad quiénes eran sus enemigos y quiénes sus aliados dentro de su propia organización.

El Cartel de Medellín en su etapa más oscura era un ecosistema de miedo, lealtades frágiles y tensión acumulada sin válvula de escape. Las fuerzas del Estado apretaban, los grupos rivales olían la sangre y dentro del cartel comenzaban a aparecer fracturas peligrosas. En ese ambiente, Popeye —el hombre más cercano al patrón, su brazo armado y su sombra— vivía sometido a una presión que ningún ser humano puede sostener indefinidamente sin consecuencias.

Aquella noche, en una guarida discreta diseñada para esconder a Escobar del mundo, una cadena de circunstancias, nervios al límite y un movimiento mal interpretado en la oscuridad estuvo a punto de cambiar la historia del narcotráfico colombiano para siempre. Todo pasó en cuestión de segundos. Y las consecuencias de ese instante marcaron a todos los presentes de por vida.

snippet.title: Gram Parsons: Der Millionenerbe, der mit 26 starb
snippet.description:
Gram Parsons erbte ein Vermögen, wurde mit 26 zur Legende des Country-Rock – und starb einsam in einem Wüstenmotel bei Joshua Tree.

Er war Erbe eines Zitrus-Imperiums aus Florida, verlor mit zwölf seinen Vater und mit achtzehn am Tag seines Schulabschlusses seine Mutter. Mit seiner Idee einer „Cosmic American Music" riss Gram Parsons die Mauer zwischen Country und Rock ein: bei den Byrds prägte er das Album „Sweetheart of the Rodeo", gründete die Flying Burrito Brothers, beeinflusste Keith Richards und die Rolling Stones und entdeckte Emmylou Harris. Drei Wochen nach Vollendung seines Meisterwerks „Grievous Angel" starb er 1973 an einer Überdosis – und sein Leichnam wurde von seinem Manager gestohlen und in der Wüste verbrannt. Erst nach seinem Tod wurde er als Vater des Country-Rock gefeiert; 2026 folgt die Aufnahme in die Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Diese Folge erzählt, wie Reichtum und Tragödie eine ganze Familie zeichneten.

snippet.description:
Al Capones Ehefrau Mae schwieg fast 30 Jahre mitten im gefürchtetsten Verbrecherimperium Amerikas – und nahm ihr Geheimnis mit ins Grab.

Mae Coughlin war eine irische Katholikin aus Brooklyn, fleißig, unauffällig, anständig. Dann heiratete sie Al Capone – und wurde zur unsichtbarsten Frau Amerikas. snippet.title: Bugsy Siegel — The Man Who Built Las Vegas and Paid With His Life
snippet.description:

snippet.description:

Dieses Video erzählt die ungeschminkte Geschichte der Capone-Frauen: Als einziger Schwester Mafalda, seiner stillen Ehefrau Mae und den Enkelinnen, die lange nach dem Zusammenbruch des Imperiums aufwuchsen.  
Wir blicken hinter die Kulissen des Hauses an der Prairie Avenue in Chicago und zeigen, was geschieht, wenn die Kameras abgezogen sind und der Gangster ins Gefängnis geht. Es ist die tragische Geschichte von Frauen, die den Namen Capone nicht gewählt haben, aber ein Leben lang seine Last trugen.

snippet.title: The Real Dutch Schultz Was The Most Dangerous Mob Boss In 'Hoodlum' Movie
snippet.description:
He controlled the Harlem numbers racket, ran the largest beer operation on the East Coast, and beat the federal government in two tax trials. Then he tried to assassinate a federal prosecutor named Thomas Dewey, and the entire National Crime Syndicate voted to kill him. This is the real story of Dutch Schultz — the Bronx kid born Arthur Flegenheimer who became the only mob boss in American history that Lucky Luciano’s Commission ever formally ordered dead.

In this Mafia deep dive, we trace Schultz’s bloody rise from teenage burglar to $20 million-a-year empire, the savage war for Harlem against Stephanie St Clair and Bumpy Johnson, the rigged numbers scheme engineered by mathematician Otto “Abbadabba” Berman, and the final 90 seconds inside the Palace Chop House on October 23, 1935.

What you will learn:
 • How Schultz and Joey Noe built a $2 million bootlegging empire by 1929
 • How Otto Berman rigged the Harlem numbers racket using racetrack mathematics
 • The brutal Harlem war between Schultz, Stephanie St Clair, and Bumpy Johnson
 • Why Schultz moved his trial to Malone, NY — and bought off an entire town
 • The Commission meeting where Schultz threatened to kill Thomas Dewey
 • The Murder Inc. hit team: Charles “The Bug” Workman, Mendy Weiss, and “Piggy”
 • Schultz’s 22 hours of delirious deathbed ravings — transcribed by police
 • The $50 million treasure still buried in the Catskills

Key figures: 
Arthur Flegenheimer (Dutch Schultz), Lucky Luciano, Thomas Dewey, Stephanie St Clair, Bumpy Johnson, Otto Berman, Bo Weinberg, Charles Workman, Albert Anastasia, Louis Lepke Buchalter.

Timeline: 
1901 birth in the Bronx → 1928 Joey Noe murder → 1931-33 Harlem numbers war → 1935 Malone tax acquittal → October 23, 1935 Palace Chop House assassination.

Why this story matters today: 
Dutch Schultz was the last great independent gangster — and his death marks the exact moment American organized crime transformed from chaotic Prohibition-era violence into the disciplined, institutional Mafia that dominated the next 70 years. His refusal to obey the Commission rewrote the rules forever.

snippet.title: The Real Mel Weinberg Was the Most Dangerous Con Man Behind 'American Hustle' Movie
snippet.description:
In 1978, the FBI hired a convicted con artist named Mel Weinberg to recover stolen paintings. Two years later, he had helped them snare a United States senator, six congressmen, a New Jersey mayor, and the biggest political corruption scandal in modern American history. This is the true story behind American Hustle. The real ABSCAM. The case Hollywood softened.

In this deep-dive documentary, we trace the real ABSCAM operation from its origins as a small art-theft investigation in Queens to its explosive transformation into a sting that filmed sitting members of Congress accepting cash bribes.

What you'll learn in this video: 
• How Mel Weinberg, a Bronx-born grifter facing federal prison for an advance-fee loan scam, became the FBI's most valuable informant 
• How FBI agent John Good built a fake Arab investment company called Abdul Enterprises out of a Long Island field office, backed by a real $1 million account at Chase Manhattan 
• How Camden Mayor Angelo Errichetti — also a NJ state senator — demanded $400,000, told the undercover team "I'll give you Atlantic City," and became the middleman who recruited the politicians 
• How six U.S. Representatives took cash (mostly $50,000; Richard Kelly took $25,000) — and how Senator Harrison Williams took a hidden stake in a phony titanium venture instead of cash 
• Why Congressman Michael "Ozzie" Myers said "money talks and bullshit walks" on tape, a quote that outlived his career 
• How the February 2, 1980 leak detonated a Washington scandal that ended the careers of six congressmen and a senator 
• What Hollywood got right and wrong about the case in David O. Russell's 2013 film American Hustle, starring Christian Bale, Amy Adams, and Bradley Cooper 
• The aftermath: Myers' expulsion (376–30), Williams' prison term, and the 1981 Civiletti Guidelines that changed FBI sting operations forever

Key figures: 
Mel Weinberg, FBI Special Agent John F. Good, FBI Agent Anthony Amoroso, Mayor Angelo Errichetti, Senator Harrison A. Williams Jr., Rep. Michael "Ozzie" Myers, Rep. John Jenrette, Rep. Frank Thompson, Rep. John Murphy, Rep. Raymond Lederer, Rep. Richard Kelly.

Why this story matters today: 
ABSCAM remains the most consequential public-corruption sting in U.S. history. It exposed how cheaply political power could be bought and reshaped how federal investigators can target elected officials. Decades later, every public-corruption sting still operates in its shadow.

Sources: 
• FBI Official History: https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/abscam 
• U.S. Senate Historical Office, Expulsion Case of Harrison A. Williams Jr. (1982): https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/expulsion/140HarrisonWilliams_expulsion.htm 
• Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Abscam": https://www.britannica.com/topic/Abscam

snippet.title: The Real Boardwalk Empire: How the Mafia Secretly Took Over Atlantic City
snippet.description:
In November of 1928, Arnold Rothstein bled out in a Manhattan hotel room and refused to name his killer. Seven months later, the most dangerous men in America gathered on the Atlantic City boardwalk to divide up the country. 

This is the real story behind HBO’s Boardwalk Empire, and it’s bloodier, richer, and stranger than the show ever dared to be.

Step inside the true history of Enoch “Nucky” Johnson, the 6 foot 4 political boss who ran Atlantic City like his personal kingdom for 30 years, earning an estimated $500,000 a year tax free at the height of Prohibition. Watch how Al Capone built a $100 million a year empire in Chicago, only to be destroyed by an accountant tracing unpaid taxes. Discover how Charlie “Lucky” Luciano restructured American organized crime forever after eliminating his two bosses in 1931, then cut a wartime deal with the U.S. Navy that walked him out of a 30 to 50 year sentence. And learn why Meyer Lansky, the quiet financial genius, was the only one who truly won.

In this documentary you will learn:
- The real events of the 1929 Atlantic City Conference and the 3 decisions that built the modern Mafia
- How Nucky Johnson controlled politicians, police, and the press for 3 decades
- The exact tax evasion case that took down Al Capone in 1931
- The shocking deal called Operation Underworld that freed Luciano during World War 2
- Why Meyer Lansky beat every charge and died wealthy in his own bed
- What HBO got right, and the brutal truths they had to leave out

Key figures covered: 
Nucky Johnson, Al Capone, Charlie “Lucky” Luciano, Meyer Lansky, Arnold Rothstein, Bugsy Siegel, Frank Costello, Thomas Dewey, Joe Masseria, and Salvatore Maranzano. Timeline: 1919 to 1983.

This story matters because the rules these men wrote on a boardwalk in May 1929 still define organized crime today. From cartel finance to political corruption, the playbook they invented is still being used.

In her own words, Farah Diba Pahlavi tells her turbulent life story, and how she became the first and only Empress in the history of Persia. The history of this country and its culture are as much the theme of this film as is the life of Farah, a role model to women in Iran.

The film goes on a journey with Empress Farah Pahlavi through her truly unique love story. It documents her life today in Paris, accompanies her to the Shah’s grave in Cairo on the anniversary of his death, and travels with her to the Biennale in Venice. 
Rich, partly unpublished archive material from all periods of Farah Pahlavi’s life, especially from Iran in the 1960s and 1970s will be included in the documentary. She will also open her private archive with many unpublished photographs as well as private amateur films.
